title: Sharp pleuritic chest pain days 2-4 after MI: peri-infarction pericarditis (overlying necrotic myocardium)
vignette: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with an acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. The patient undergoes coronary angiography with stent placement in the left circumflex artery, and he is started on therapy with a beta blocker and antiplatelet agents. On day 3 of hospitalization he experiences chest pain. The pain, described as sharp and radiating to his neck and shoulders, is exacerbated by coughing and swallowing. He has no shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or abdominal pain. Temperature is 37.5 C (99.5 F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min and regular, and respirations are 20/min. The lungs are clear on auscultation. There is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's chest pain?

clues.note: A transmural (STEMI) infarct causes myocardial necrosis extending to the epicardial surface - the substrate for early post-MI pericarditis.

clues.text: On day 3 of hospitalization he experiences chest pain
clues.note: Peri-infarction pericarditis typically develops 2-4 days after a transmural MI (early), unlike Dressler syndrome (weeks to months).

clues.text: sharp and radiating to his neck and shoulders, is exacerbated by coughing and swallowing
clues.note: Sharp, PLEURITIC/positional chest pain radiating to the neck/shoulder and worsened by coughing/swallowing is characteristic of PERICARDITIS (not ischemia).

whatMatters: Sharp, pleuritic/positional chest pain 2-4 days after a transmural (ST-elevation) MI = PERI-INFARCTION PERICARDITIS: fibrinous/serofibrinous inflammation of the pericardium OVERLYING the NECROTIC myocardial segment. Answer C.
strategy: Contrast pericarditis with re-ischemia: sharp, pleuritic, positional pain worse with coughing/swallowing (radiating to neck/shoulder) + low-grade fever = pericarditis, NOT the crushing constant pain of ischemia. Timing 2-4 days after transmural MI = peri-infarction pericarditis, localized to the necrotic segment. Reject autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue (Dressler syndrome - weeks-months, diffuse), viral pericarditis (URI prodrome, less likely as a direct MI complication), and recurrent/nonculprit coronary thrombosis (would reproduce anginal, crushing pain).

options.text: Pericardial inflammation due to autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue
Pericardial inflammation due to concomitant viral infection
Pericardial inflammation overlying the necrotic segment of myocardium
Recurrent thrombosis of the culprit coronary vessel
Thrombosis of a nonculprit coronary vessel

eliminations.label: Autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue - Dressler (weeks-months)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: Dressler (postcardiac injury) syndrome, an autoimmune pericarditis from antigens exposed by infarction. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: Dressler occurs LATER (a week to months after MI) and diffusely; day-3 pain fits peri-infarction pericarditis. ✅ Correct if: pericarditis weeks-months post-MI (Dressler).

eliminations.label: Concomitant viral infection - less likely post-MI
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: viral pericarditis (often after a URI). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: there's no viral prodrome, and pericarditis here is a direct complication of the transmural MI, not viral. ✅ Correct if: pericarditis after an upper respiratory illness.

eliminations.label: Recurrent thrombosis of culprit vessel - anginal pain
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: re-occlusion of the stented (culprit) vessel. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: stent thrombosis/re-ischemia causes CRUSHING, constant anginal pain, not sharp pleuritic/positional pain worsened by swallowing. ✅ Correct if: recurrent ischemic chest pain with ECG changes/troponin rise.

eliminations.label: Thrombosis of a nonculprit vessel - anginal pain
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a new infarct in a different coronary artery. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it would produce ischemic (crushing, exertional/constant) pain, not pleuritic pericardial pain. ✅ Correct if: new territory ischemia/infarction.

reasoning: The pain is sharp, pleuritic/positional, radiates to neck/shoulders, and worsens with coughing/swallowing = pericarditis
It appears on day 3 after a transmural (ST-elevation) MI
This timing/localization fits fibrinous inflammation of the pericardium overlying the necrotic myocardium
mechanism: After a TRANSMURAL (ST-ELEVATION) MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION, necrosis extends to the EPICARDIAL surface and incites a localized FIBRINOUS/serofibrinous inflammatory reaction of the overlying PERICARDIUM - PERI-INFARCTION PERICARDITIS (PIP), which develops in ~10-20% of patients typically 2-4 DAYS post-MI (delayed reperfusion/larger necrosis increases risk). The pain is PLEURITIC and POSITIONAL: sharp, worse with inspiration/coughing/SWALLOWING and often relieved by sitting forward, sometimes radiating to the neck/shoulders (diaphragmatic/phrenic afferents), and may be accompanied by low-grade fever and a friction rub - distinct from the crushing, constant pain of ISCHEMIA. PIP is usually self-limited and treated supportively (sometimes high-dose aspirin). It differs from DRESSLER (postcardiac injury) SYNDROME, an autoimmune pericarditis occurring a WEEK TO MONTHS after MI with diffuse pericardial involvement. Recurrent or nonculprit coronary thrombosis would cause anginal (ischemic) pain, and viral pericarditis follows a URI - neither fits this early post-MI pleuritic pain overlying the infarct.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid CV > post-MI pericarditis: peri-infarction pericarditis (PIP) 2-4 days after transmural MI (fibrinous, overlying necrosis); Dressler syndrome weeks-months (autoimmune, diffuse); pleuritic/positional chest pain, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Sharp pleuritic pain 2-4 days post-transmural MI = peri-infarction pericarditis over the necrotic segment.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on peri-infarction pericarditis, Dressler syndrome, pleuritic vs ischemic pain, transmural MI, or friction rub? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Dressler = weeks-months (autoimmune); viral = URI prodrome; recurrent/nonculprit thrombosis = crushing anginal pain.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: pleuritic chest pain 2-4 days after transmural MI = peri-infarction pericarditis; Dressler = weeks-months later.

keywords.back: Sharp, pleuritic, positional (worse lying/coughing/swallowing; better sitting forward)
Necrosis to epicardium -> overlying pericardial inflammation

firstAid.detail: CV: fibrinous inflammation over infarct, days 2-4 post-MI.

memoryHook: Sharp pain that hurts to cough/swallow a few days after a big MI = the pericardium over the dead muscle getting inflamed (peri-infarction pericarditis) - Dressler comes weeks later.
